---
title: "The packages"
description: "What each package is for, what it deliberately leaves alone, and where the seams are."
---

Three packages, three jobs. The division is not arbitrary: each one stops where
its evidence stops.

## splitGraph {#splitgraph}

[Documentation](https://selcukorkmaz.github.io/splitGraph/) ·
[Source](https://github.com/selcukorkmaz/splitGraph) ·
[CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=splitGraph)

**Represent dataset structure so that leakage-relevant relationships are
explicit, validated, and queryable.**

A metadata table becomes a typed dependency graph: `Sample` nodes linked to
`Subject`, `Batch`, `Study`, `Site`, `Region`, `Platform`, `Assay`, `Timepoint`,
`FeatureSet` and `Outcome` nodes by typed edges. Once the structure is an
object, it can be validated, queried, and turned into deterministic split
constraints.

| Stage | Functions |
|---|---|
| Build | `graph_from_metadata()`, `ingest_metadata()`, `create_nodes()`, `build_dependency_graph()` |
| Validate | `validate_graph()`, `depgraph_validation_report()` |
| Query | `query_node_type()`, `query_paths()`, shared-dependency helpers |
| Derive | `derive_split_constraints()`, `pairwise_edges()` |
| Interchange | `as_split_spec()`, `write_split_spec()`, `validate_json()`, `migrate_json()` |

**What it will not do.** It does not fit models, run preprocessing, or generate
resamples. That boundary is the point: the graph describes the dataset, and
something else decides what to do about it.

**The seam.** `as_split_spec()` produces a `split_spec` — a versioned,
sample-keyed contract with `group_var`, `block_vars`, `time_var` and
`stratum_var`. `write_split_spec()` serialises it to JSON against a schema
shipped in the package, which is how a split definition reaches a Python
collaborator without either side reimplementing the other's logic.

## bioLeak {#bioleak}

[Documentation](https://selcukorkmaz.github.io/bioLeak/) ·
[Source](https://github.com/selcukorkmaz/bioLeak) ·
[CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bioLeak)

**Enforce leakage-resistant evaluation, then produce evidence about what is
left.**

bioLeak covers the two halves that a structural description cannot: building
folds that actually respect the structure, and measuring how much apparent
performance survives when the structure is controlled for.

| Stage | Functions |
|---|---|
| Splits | `as_leaksplits()`, `make_split_plan()`, `check_split_overlap()`, `as_rsample()` |
| Guarded fitting | `fit_resample()`, `tune_resample()`, `impute_guarded()`, `guard_to_recipe()`, `predict_guard()` |
| Auditing | `audit_leakage()`, `audit_leakage_by_learner()`, `audit_report()`, `calibration_summary()`, `confounder_sensitivity()`, `delta_lsi()`, `cv_ci()` |
| Plots | `plot_perm_distribution()`, `plot_fold_balance()`, `plot_overlap_checks()`, `plot_calibration()`, `plot_time_acf()`, `plot_confounder_sensitivity()` |
| Simulation | `simulate_leakage_suite()`, `benchmark_leakage_suite()` |

Split modes are `subject_grouped`, `batch_blocked`, `study_loocv`,
`time_series` (with `purge` and `embargo`), and `combined` for several axes at
once. Guarded preprocessing means imputation, normalisation, filtering and
feature selection are re-estimated inside each training fold rather than once
over the whole dataset.

**What it will not do.** It does not prove that a dataset is leak-free. The
audit produces evidence — a permutation gap, an association test, a duplicate
count — and evidence is not a proof.

**The seams.** `as_leaksplits()` takes a splitGraph `split_spec` and builds
folds from it directly, so the structure never has to be restated by hand.
`as_rsample()` converts the resulting `LeakSplits` into an `rsample` `rset`,
which is the lingua franca for everything downstream in tidymodels.

## fastml {#fastml}

[Documentation](https://selcukorkmaz.github.io/fastml/) ·
[Tutorial](https://selcukorkmaz.github.io/fastml-tutorial/) ·
[Source](https://github.com/selcukorkmaz/fastml) ·
[CRAN](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=fastml)

**Train, tune and compare many models without letting preprocessing leak back
in at the last step.**

In fastml, *fast* refers to how quickly you can assemble a statistically valid
workflow, not to computational shortcuts. A single `fastml()` call trains a set
of algorithms, coordinating preprocessing, fitting and evaluation inside the
resampling path so that the comparison between models stays honest.

| Stage | Functions |
|---|---|
| Fit and compare | `fastml()`, `train_models()`, `availableMethods()` |
| Explore and explain | `fastexplore()`, `fastexplain()`, `explain_dalex()`, `explain_lime()`, `explain_ale()`, `plot_ice()`, `surrogate_tree()`, `counterfactual_explain()` |
| Inspect | `summary()`, `plot()`, `get_best_model_names()`, `get_best_workflows()` |
| Defaults and tuning | `compare_defaults()`, `get_default_differences()`, `recommend_tuning_config()`, `estimate_tuning_time()` |
| Persist | `save_fastml()`, `load_model()` |

Built-in resampling covers `cv`, `repeatedcv`, `grouped_cv`, `blocked_cv`,
`rolling_origin`, `nested_cv`, `boot` and `validation_split`. The `resamples =`
argument takes an `rsample` object directly, which is how folds built upstream
get used unchanged.

**What it will not do.** It does not introduce new learning algorithms, and it
does not modify the statistical behaviour of the engines it orchestrates
(`recipes`, `rsample`, `parsnip`, `yardstick`). It also cannot stop you handing
it data you already preprocessed globally — a guarded workflow only guards the
part it runs.

## How they compose

| | splitGraph | bioLeak | fastml |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Describes dataset structure | ● | ○ | |
| Validates structural assumptions | ● | ○ | |
| Builds folds | | ● | ● |
| Guarded preprocessing inside folds | | ● | ● |
| Post-hoc leakage evidence | | ● | |
| Trains and compares many models | | ○ | ● |
| Model explanation | | | ● |
| Cross-language handoff | ● | | |

: ● primary job  ○ partial or secondary {tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

The overlap between bioLeak and fastml on fold construction is real and
intentional. bioLeak builds folds when the split policy itself is the object of
study; fastml builds them when you simply want a sound default and the
modelling is the point. The [worked example](get-started.qmd) uses bioLeak's
folds inside fastml, which is the case where you want both.
